metadata.title: The House Is a Witness.
metadata.topic: How the art, sound and music of HOUSEGHOST were designed, generated and wired into Godot
metadata.author: Narasimha Reddy Valam

beats.role_note: Walker bookend 1 — Claude composer.
beats.narration_text: Aloha, this is Liam, in for Bear. Today we take apart HOUSEGHOST, a Godot game by Narasimha Reddy Valam about a boy nobody is looking for, and the one key that turns his world over.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about HOUSEGHOST — you play the ghost of a boy the world believes ran away. One key turns the world over. Build the Night 1 slice.

beats.role_note: Walker bookend 2 — hesitant summary, one word corrected.
beats.narration_text: One bedroom, two versions of it, and one verb. Walk, jump, turn the room over, reach for something that was yours. Seven nights, three relics, and a child in the doorway who is the only witness the game has.

beats.role_note: FULL SCREEN — the storyboard, all six panels, explained.
beats.narration_text: The drawings came first. Six panels, committed five days before a single image was generated. Three shot sizes — wide, medium, close-up — and four camera angles, eye level through a Dutch tilt, in one frame shape throughout. They run on a colour rule taken from the game rather than from taste: grey is the truth, amber is the memory, and yellow is the one living person who can see him. Panels one and six carry no colour at all. That rule is also the acceptance test — amber in the wrong place is a failed generation, not a style choice.

props.title: The drawings came first.
props.status: Six panels · three shot sizes · four angles · committed 2026-10-01

beats.role_note: FULL SCREEN — the character sheet as a contract.
beats.narration_text: The character sheet is the specification every generated image had to meet. The silhouette is tested at thirty-three by ninety-six pixels, the size he actually appears on screen, because detail that disappears at game size is not detail. One collision capsule, fifty-two by two hundred and fifty, identical in every pose and in both states. A five-colour palette checked against the room so he never vanishes into it. And the consistency rules that let a generation be judged rather than merely liked: proportions, eye position, outline weight, and the silhouette itself.

props.title: The sheet is the contract.
props.source: design/character/ · SOURCES.md rows CHAR-REF and CHAR-WALK8

beats.role_note: FULL SCREEN — the required design-to-game trace, five steps.
beats.narration_text: Here is one asset, end to end. The sheet. The prompt, shown verbatim, asking for a flat magenta backdrop — because asking a model for a transparent background returns a drawn checkerboard. The raw output, untouched. The chroma key: magenta-ness is the minimum of red and blue, minus green, with a soft alpha and a de-spill. And the result, running in the engine at thirty-three by ninety-six.

beats.role_note: FULL SCREEN — the three failed measures.
beats.narration_text: Getting those frames to one size failed three times. Matching height failed, because a crouch is shorter than a stand. Matching shoulder width failed, because raised arms move the shoulders. Matching head width failed on the rising pose, where the topmost pixels are not his head — they are his hands. Body area worked. Every obvious measure turned out to be a property of the pose rather than of the boy.

props.title: Three measures that failed.
props.status: Height · shoulders · head width · body area

beats.role_note: FULL SCREEN — rejections as evidence of judgment.
beats.narration_text: The takes that lost are kept. One boy carried less detail than the sheet specifies. A storyboard panel was turned down because a lamp had drifted from the room established two panels earlier, which only becomes visible once the earlier panels exist to disagree with. And one model was dropped altogether after it kept returning a storybook schoolchild.

props.title: The takes that lost.
props.status: Four rejections, each judged against the sheet

qc.contrast_reason: The figure in this beat is a contact sheet of rejected generations. Those are screenshots of model output and several carry small labels baked into the image by the model itself — image pixels, not typography this film authored. The regions declared here are the designed text: the beat title and the cue cards, both ink on cream. My own captions inside the figure were darkened to ink as well, which did not clear the finding, confirming the flagged blobs are inside the thumbnails rather than mine.

beats.role_note: CODE → RESULT. flip() at reading size.
beats.narration_text: Here is the function that turns the world over. State first, signal second, sound third. That order holds everywhere: audio is a consequence, never a cause, so muting it cannot change what the game does. And the guard on the first line is not decoration — hold the key down and the flipping flag refuses the second call, so one turn makes exactly one sound.

props.title: One turn, one sound.
props.code:
func flip() -> void:
	if _flipping or _meters.ended:
		return
	_flipping = true
	is_inverted = not is_inverted

	world_flipped.emit(is_inverted)
	_audio.play("flip")

beats.role_note: CODE → RESULT. The cause-and-effect beat: the mix table.
beats.narration_text: A pass over the mix found the problem was not the levels that were set. It was the ones that were never set. Three sounds — the footsteps, the ghost's drift and the fall — were missing from this table, so they played at full level while the comment above it claimed footsteps were deliberately quiet. Matched peaks are not matched loudness: at equal peaks the steps sat five decibels above the flip. The loudest sound in the game was the one that fires most often.

props.title: The levels that were never set.
props.code:
const LEVELS := {
	"flip":     -3.0,
	"contact":  -3.0,
	"frost":    -3.0,
	"correct":  -5.0,
	"land":    -11.0,
	"jump":    -13.0,
	"fall":     -9.0,    ## a death: still the loudest thing here, deliberately
	"step":     -9.0,    ## constant, so it sits well under every story beat
	"ghoststep": -11.0,  ## quieter again; he is not meant to sound solid
}

beats.role_note: Four spine sounds in real play.
beats.narration_text: Nine sounds carry this slice and four are the spine: turning the world over, a contact landing, a day tearing off the calendar, and falling out of the world. Each fires from a signal the game emits after it has already changed state, and each fires once. Holding the key or mashing it does not stack them.

beats.role_note: CODE → RESULT. The Ogg loop flag.
beats.narration_text: The music ships as Ogg Vorbis. Converting the files was not the whole job — Godot's importer defaults loop to false, and Ogg and WAV spell looping differently. Swap the extensions alone and the score plays once and stops.

props.title: The importer says false.

beats.role_note: Visible result of B14 — the recorded check.
beats.narration_text: Thirteen automated assertions, zero failures. They count each sound against each event under rapid repeats and held input, and confirm that muting changes no game state. They were also green through every real fault this game had: green while the player could not move, green while three sounds could not be heard, green while a clean clone printed load errors. Passing tests and a broken game are not a contradiction. They measure different things.

beats.role_note: Verdict — built, and not yet built.
beats.narration_text: So what is here. Two character states, both versions of the room, three relics, seven nights, gravity inversion, nine sound events, two music loops, separate mutes, and a girl whose posture is the recognition meter. Not yet: the hallway that rearranges itself and the cellar door are drawn and belong to later nights. Three sheet poses are specified and ungenerated. And the relic cues have not been tried on a fresh player.

beats.role_note: Contributions and models — required content.
beats.narration_text: HOUSEGHOST is designed, built and verified by Narasimha Reddy Valam. The game is his: the story, the inversion, the seven nights, and the decision that a child's posture should carry the meter instead of a number. He generated every image, every sound effect and both music loops, judged each against his own sheet, and threw out the ones that missed. He played it with the sound on, and then with all of it off. Claude Code was the tool at the keyboard. The art came from ChatGPT's image model, the music from Suno under non-commercial terms, the sound effects from ElevenLabs. Gemini was tried for the character and did not make it in.

artifactLines: Narasimha Reddy Valam — design, story, every generation, every rejection, the playtest.
ChatGPT image model — character, rooms, relics, storyboard.
Suno v6-mini — two music loops, non-commercial.

beats.role_note: Your Turn — one bounded change and a prediction.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Please use Walker to add a relic reachable only by falling upward through a ceiling gap, and predict what it does to the night count before you run it. Write the prediction down first. If the calendar disagrees with you, the interesting thing is not the bug — it is the distance between what you expected and what the engine did. That has been Liam, in for Bear.
